HyperCard product and later interviews on HyperCard's origin (citation from model recall)"],"universe_relevance_clue":"Task results and design-seed packs are card-like atoms: small, named, sequenced, and potentially authorable by non-engineers.","inference_or_causal_reading":"A small information atom plus light scripting produced an explosion of end-user software; weak persistence and organizational ownership ended it.","uncertainty":"HyperTalk syntax, HyperCard 2.x feature boundaries, and relations to later OpenDoc are recalled loosely.","provenance":"MODEL_RECALL"},{"observed_example_or_era":"Larry Tesler modeless text editing and cut-copy-paste, Xerox PARC through Macintosh, 1970s–1984","observation":"Select-then-verb editing with a global clipboard replaced sticky input modes that users forgot they were in.","problem_addressed":"Modal editors caused predictable errors: commands meant for one mode executed in another, and the current mode was easy to lose.","enabling_constraints_or_technology":"Mouse-driven selection, a named paste buffer, dedicated key chords, and GUI applications that could share a system clipboard.","interaction_form":"Modeless typing; selection as the object of the next verb; cut, copy, paste as a transferable intermediate object.","contemporary_reaction_or_critique":"Widely adopted and treated as obvious in hindsight; critics later noted that modal dialogs and app modes returned, and that an invisible clipboard is itself hidden state.","suspected_source_or_example":"Gypsy and Smalltalk editing at PARC; Macintosh desk accessories and Edit menu as the mass-market form.","source_references":["Tesler, L. A Personal History of Modeless Text Editing and Cut/Copy/Paste. interactions, 2012 (citation from model recall)","Tesler, L. The Smalltalk Environment. BYTE, August 1981 (citation from model recall)"],"universe_relevance_clue":"Hidden worker or conductor modes are a reliability hazard; intermediate results should appear as explicit objects rather than as an invisible clipboard.","inference_or_causal_reading":"Implicit interaction state produces operator error; making the object of action visible, then applying a verb, remains the safer default.","uncertainty":"Exact Tesler quotations and which PARC system first shipped a given clipboard behavior are paraphrased from recall.","provenance":"MODEL_RECALL"},{"observed_example_or_era":"Palm Pilot and Palm OS, 1996–early 2000s","observation":"A pocket computer did a few tasks instantly, wrote with a constrained alphabet, and treated the desktop cradle as source of truth.","problem_addressed":"Newton and other early PDAs were too ambitious, too slow, and too disconnected from the PC where real data already lived.","enabling_constraints_or_technology":"Severe RAM/CPU limits, monochrome LCD, Graffiti recognizer, hardware app buttons, and HotSync as a bounded replication protocol.","interaction_form":"Instant-on launcher, short forms, dedicated writing area, and sync-as-commit rather than fully autonomous mobile authorship.","contemporary_reaction_or_critique":"Praised for restraint and reliability; Graffiti had a learning curve; later Palms over-expanded and were displaced by phones that absorbed the companion role.","suspected_source_or_example":"Palm Pilot 1000/5000 and Palm OS PIM suite; contrast with Apple Newton MessagePad.","source_references":["Butter, A. and Pogue, D. Piloting Palm. Wiley, 2002 (citation from model recall)","Hawkins, D. interviews on Palm design constraints (citation from model recall)"],"universe_relevance_clue":"A mobile conductor can be a constrained companion that syncs bounded work instead of hosting the whole universe on-device.","inference_or_causal_reading":"Severe constraints plus an explicit sync contract produced habit and trust; feature maximalism later undid the advantage.","uncertainty":"Hardware specs, Graffiti recognition details, and exact HotSync conflict rules are approximate.","provenance":"MODEL_RECALL"},{"observed_example_or_era":"Apple iPhone multi-touch and full-screen applications, 2007","observation":"Finger-scale direct manipulation, inertial scrolling, and a hardware Home escape made each app a full-screen mode inside one consistent physical vocabulary.","problem_addressed":"Smartphones were cramped, stylus-driven, and inconsistent, with window chrome and hardware keyboards consuming scarce attention and space.","enabling_constraints_or_technology":"Capacitive multi-touch, mobile ARM performance, gesture recognizers, and a capacitive slab with one reliable out control.","interaction_form":"Direct finger manipulation, gestures, full-screen app as mode, Home as escape hatch, later an app store as the extension mechanism.","contemporary_reaction_or_critique":"Acclaimed for fluidity; criticized for killing hardware keyboards, reintroducing apps as modes, and enclosing software in a walled garden.","suspected_source_or_example":"iPhone 1 / iPhone OS; earlier multi-touch research at FingerWorks and academic labs as enabling lineage.","source_references":["Jobs, S. iPhone introduction, Macworld, January 2007 (citation from model recall)","Apple Human Interface Guidelines for iPhone OS (citation from model recall of published HIG themes)"],"universe_relevance_clue":"Isolated full-screen work surfaces plus a single escape to a conductor home map onto task-frame isolation with a reliable return path.","inference_or_causal_reading":"One consistent physical vocabulary plus a trustworthy out control made a modal application model acceptable on a tiny display.","uncertainty":"Early gesture sets, first-year OS boundaries, and which multi-touch patents mattered most are recalled approximately.","provenance":"MODEL_RECALL"},{"observed_example_or_era":"General Magic Magic Cap and Telescript mobile agents, early-to-mid 1990s","observation":"Handheld networked services were imagined as places and traveling agents: desks, hallways, post offices, stamps, and code that moved with bounded authority.","problem_addressed":"A fat always-on client could not be assumed; services had to cross devices and networks as emissaries rather than as a single local application.","enabling_constraints_or_technology":"Agent-oriented language (Telescript), scene-based metaphorical UI, early personal communicators, and premature wireless/infrastructure.","interaction_form":"Room-like scenes, objects you can send, agents that go elsewhere and return with results, permission and place as part of the interaction model.","contemporary_reaction_or_critique":"Seen as too metaphorical and too early; commercial failure at the time, later treated as prophetic for mobile agents, smartphones, and cloud services.","suspected_source_or_example":"Magic Cap UI; Telescript agent language and white papers; Sony Magic Link / Motorola Envoy class devices.","source_references":["White, J.E. Telescript Technology: Mobile Agents (General Magic papers, citation from model recall)","Hertzfeld, A. and General Magic participant accounts of Magic Cap (citation from model recall)","Magic Cap user-interface scene model as described in period product coverage (citation from model recall)"],"universe_relevance_clue":"A conductor dispatching isolated workers across a network with bounded authority is a direct conceptual ancestor of task-frame sub-workers.","inference_or_causal_reading":"Mobile code with explicit places and permissions is a powerful composition model, but a heavy metaphor and premature networks can hide the architecture from users and markets.","uncertainty":"Telescript instruction details and Magic Cap screen sequences are recalled at documentary/summary level, not from primary manuals.","provenance":"MODEL_RECALL"},{"observed_example_or_era":"Rooms virtual workspaces (Henderson and Card), 1986, on Xerox window systems","observation":"Window clutter was treated as space contention across tasks: users switched among named rooms that clustered windows by activity rather than by application.","problem_addressed":"Overlapping windows scaled poorly as task count grew; users lost work and spent effort on window housekeeping instead of the task.","enabling_constraints_or_technology":"Bitmap window systems, virtual desktop spaces, overview maps, and research window managers that could hold multiple workspaces.","interaction_form":"Named rooms, doors or switches between rooms, overviews of room contents, and task-clustered window sets.","contemporary_reaction_or_critique":"Influential in HCI; later virtual desktops were often underused because users forgot room contents or found switching cost higher than expected.","suspected_source_or_example":"Henderson and Card Rooms; later virtual-desktop features in mainstream window managers as diluted descendants.","source_references":["Henderson, D.A. Jr. and Card, S. Rooms: The Use of Multiple Virtual Workspaces to Reduce Space Contention in a Window-Based Graphical User Interface. ACM Transactions on Graphics, 1986 (venue recalled; citation from model recall)"],"universe_relevance_clue":"Task frames can act as rooms that isolate contention; an overview of frames is a room map rather than a flat log.","inference_or_causal_reading":"Space contention is cognitive as well as display-bound; clustering by task beats clustering by application when several jobs coexist.","uncertainty":"Paper venue labeling (TOG versus related ACM venues) and the Cedar/Rooms implementation name may be slightly misremembered.","provenance":"MODEL_RECALL"}]}
